text: How do you approach a negotiation about price?

speaker: You
text: I try never to concede anything without it buying something. If a buyer asks for a lower price, the answer is not yes or no — it is yes, if you commit to this volume . The shape is always the same and using it every time trains the other side to expect it. I also decide in advance which single thing I will not move on, and I say that one plainly. In my experience if you declare exactly one immovable clause, nobody argues about it. If you declare four, everything is negotiable.

speaker: Rana Darwish
text: What do you look for when you read a contract?

speaker: You
text: Not the commercial terms, usually — those were agreed before the document arrived and they are easy to check. I look for three procedural clauses. Which document wins if two disagree, because that decides every later argument. Whether they can hand the contract to somebody else without asking me, because that could be a competitor. And whether there is any time to fix a problem before it becomes terminal. A contract with no remedy period makes one late delivery enough to end the relationship.

speaker: You
text: I ask the person at the counter, and I ask differently from most people. I say why I am asking — that I have been sent away before — so it is worth their time. Then I read the whole list back and ask whether that is all of it, which is where they add the thing nobody thinks to ask about. And I always ask what happens if something is wrong, because the expensive rules live in the failure case. The last time I did that I learned that a pen correction voids a document.

speaker: Nour Haddad
text: What makes a meeting useful?

speaker: You
text: An agenda that went out beforehand, with each item marked for what it needs — decision, discussion or information. People prepare differently when they know which it is. Then a chair who closes each item rather than letting it drift, and who is willing to say that nothing is going to be decided today. And minutes within two days that record decisions rather than discussion, with a name and a date on every action. The thing that wastes most time is not long discussions; it is items coming back a second time because nobody wrote down what happened to them.

speaker: Rana Darwish
text: Have you ever taken minutes? What did you learn?

speaker: You
text: Yes, for about two years. What I learned is that minutes record what was decided, not what was said. Nobody ever reads a transcript, and a decision with no record gets taken again six months later. Almost every minute I wrote was one of three shapes: a decision in the passive, so it belongs to the room rather than to whoever argued for it; an action with a name and a date; or a line saying an item was discussed and nothing was decided, which stops it coming back as though it had been settled.

speaker: Nour Haddad
text: How do you find your way in a building you have never visited?

speaker: You
text: I tell the person at the desk that I have not been there before, which changes the version of the directions I get. Then I say them back — floor, direction, door — and I keep the negative, because directions almost always contain one thing to avoid and that is the part people drop. I ask what to do if the person I am meeting is not there, which usually produces somewhere better to wait than a corridor. It takes about forty seconds and it means I arrive once instead of twice.

speaker: Rana Darwish
text: Should everything be written down, or do some things work better spoken?

speaker: You
text: Decisions and actions get written down, always, because memories differ within about a fortnight and nobody argues with a document circulated two days afterwards. speaker: Nour Haddad
text: Describe a process you are responsible for.

speaker: You
text: Woven cotton is inspected after finishing and before dispatch. The batch is booked in, the customer specification is drawn from the file, and five per cent is sampled at random across the full width and length — never from one end, because a run can drift. Even then the field was filled in and never looked at, which is not a control — a record nobody reads is just paper. speaker: Nour Haddad
text: How do you decide whether to tender for something?

speaker: You
text: I read two things before anything else. First the mandatory requirements, because a tender that fails one of them is not scored at all — not ranked, not read. Second the weightings, because they tell me what the client is actually buying. On the Barada tender price carried forty points and everything else sixty, which meant a discount was close to worthless and our sample length was worth two days of work. If the weights are all on price and we are not the cheapest workshop in the country, I would rather decline early and say why.

speaker: Rana Darwish
text: Tell me about a proposal you were involved in.

speaker: You
text: We tendered for bed linen for a six-hotel group this summer. My part was the lead-time section, and the useful thing in it was not the four weeks — it was the sentence saying we could not hold four weeks through July, and proposing six. A colleague found the real trap: an order taken on the twenty-eighth of June would land in the closure, so we wrote a rule that anything after the fifteenth gets the July figure. We put that in the tender rather than in our heads. I would rather be believed in eleven months than admired in one.

speaker: Nour Haddad
text: How do you explain something to a colleague so that they can use it?

speaker: You
text: I give the figure and one reason, and nothing else. Two thousand metres minimum is repeatable; two thousand metres because a dye bath below that will not hold shade is defensible, and the second one survives a buyer pushing back. Then I test it, and not by asking whether they understood — everybody says yes to that. I ask them to say it to somebody else while I listen. If they ask me to write it down, I say: you write it and I will check it. Writing it is where you find out what you did not understand.

speaker: Rana Darwish
text: Is it ever worth telling a client something that weakens your own proposal?

speaker: You
text: Almost always, if they would find it out anyway. Our July closure was going to be discovered either by us in the tender or by them in July, and the second version costs a contract rather than a point. Saying it also makes the other eleven months believable, which is the part nobody expects. What I would not do is volunteer a weakness nobody will ever meet, because that is not honesty, it is just a worse document. The test I use is simple: will this reach them later? If yes, it goes in now, in my words.
